tier_definition.D: high severity: an internal contradiction the document cannot explain away
tier_definition.C: medium severity: a defect that needs an author decision or a source to settle
tier_definition.B: low severity: a coverage or hygiene gap, not a wrong number
tier_definition.note: SPEC.md item 4.8 names 'tier-D defects' without defining the scale; this mapping is the engine's stated definition.

findings.statement: Revenue is shown as $359,490.34 but its 2 components sum to 350,490.34, a gap of 9,000 against a rounding allowance of only 0.015.
3 extraction pass(es) do not apply to a html document (ocr, pdf_text_layer, xlsx_sheets), which is expected and is recorded so the run's coverage can be read in full.
2 figures have no unit recorded, so unit and scale checks cannot reach them.

checks_run.description: Two tables that partition the same metric and period do not total the same amount.
A stated absolute or point change does not equal the difference between the two levels the ledger holds for the same metric.
A percent change and the two levels behind it point in opposite directions.
One component is claimed by two different totals in the same table column, so it is counted twice.
A component sits in a column that has a total, but no total claims it.
A stated percent change does not match the two levels it is drawn from, after first-order propagation of both levels' rounding envelopes.
A stated share of total does not equal the component divided by the total, after propagating both rounding envelopes through the quotient.
A total lists itself among its own components.
A set of composition shares does not sum to 100 within the summed rounding envelope of the shares.
The rendered value carries a negative convention that the parsed value does not, or the reverse.
A total agrees with its immediate subtotals but not with the components those subtotals are built from.
A total or subtotal differs from its components by more than the propagated rounding envelope of the whole set.
A total's discrepancy against its components exceeds the total's own display envelope but stays inside the summed envelope of the parts: the column does not foot at the precision shown.
A displayed value could not be parsed to a number, so nothing about it is checkable.
One claim carries both a growth word and a decline word.
A growth word sits on a negative move, or a decline word sits on a positive move.
A metric is called flat while the move is larger than the display could hide.
A movement word sits on a change that rounds to zero at the precision shown.
A metric is described as improved while it moved in the direction its polarity calls worse.
A metric is judged as improved or worsened but carries no polarity, so the judgement is unverifiable.
A metric is described as worsened while it moved in the direction its polarity calls better.
A prose sentence asserts a direction that the table cell for the same metric contradicts.
A causal assertion has no cause and effect pair of claims behind it.
A flow figure carries no period, so it cannot be tied to a window.
A comparative or superlative sentence carries no figure at all.
A claim's declared confidence level does not follow from its evidence basis.
A figure sits inside a forward-looking statement. Recorded for context only: a forecast is a decision, not a defect.
A prose block states a figure that is not present as any claim, so the figure is outside every check the engine can run.
A superlative has no comparable sibling values in the ledger, so it cannot be tested even in principle.
A figure in a format that supports per-cell traceability carries no source reference.
A comparison names a base period identical to the claim's own period.
A comparison sets two windows of different lengths against each other.
The document states a period that no claim covers.
A window ends after the document was extracted, so it covers data that did not exist yet.
A period's declared kind does not match the shape of its label.
A period label states a window length that the recorded length contradicts.
A window's recorded length does not match its start and end dates.
One table column mixes periods, so its rows are not comparable.
A total adds components covering different periods.
One figure is attributed to two windows of different lengths, so the same number is presented as covering both.
A trailing-window year-over-year comparison is shifted 365 days, which breaks day-of-week alignment.
A trailing-window year-over-year comparison does not record its alignment, so whether day-of-week was preserved is unknown.
A stated change is smaller than the rounding envelope of the levels it was computed from, so it is noise from the display.
Rounding the parsed value at its own displayed precision does not reproduce the rendered figure.
The extractor's declared rounding envelope does not follow from the displayed precision and scale.
One table column shows the same unit at more than one precision.
A total is displayed to a finer precision than any of its components, claiming accuracy its inputs do not carry.
A figure has no displayed precision, so no tolerance band can be built for it.
A count or a large-scale figure is shown to a precision the underlying quantity cannot have.
A value below a threshold is displayed as a number that reaches it, so the display asserts an attainment the value does not support.
A table declares a scale that its values do not honour.
A table declares a scope that its own rows contradict.
A table declares a sort order that its rows do not follow.
Two figures for the same metric and period state different filters but are presented as comparable.
A table's declared row count does not match the rows the ledger holds for it.
A superlative names a value that is not the extreme of its comparable set.
A table promising a top or bottom N does not contain N rows.
A top or bottom N table omits a value from elsewhere in the document that belongs in it.
An extraction detector reported an error or an unsupported format, so part of the document was never read.
Two claims occupy the same table cell, so the extraction or the document has a duplicated figure.
Two prose blocks carry identical text.
A table row carries no values at all beyond its own row number, so it is an unfilled template row that shipped.
A figure position renders as a dash, blank or n/a rather than a number.
The extraction report omits a coverage field, so what the extractor attempted cannot be told from what it found.
Placeholder or template markup survived into the delivered document.
The same sentence appears in more than one section.
A spreadsheet error string was rendered as a figure.
Prose names a period that no figure in the document covers, which is the signature of text carried over from a previous run.
Charts in the document could not be read, so their figures are outside every check.
A basis-points figure has a magnitude that reads as percent, or a percent figure has a magnitude that reads as basis points.
Two tables that partition the same metric and period disagree by a factor of a thousand, so one of them did not honour its declared scale.
A currency figure carries no currency code.
A figure declares a large scale but carries a value too small for that scale to have been applied.
A currency total sums components in more than one currency.
One table column mixes units, so its values cannot be read against each other.
A total sums components of more than one unit.
A percent sign is rendered on a figure whose unit is not a percentage, or the reverse.
A move in a percent-unit metric is stated as a percent change when it is a point change, or the reverse.
A ratio between 0 and 1 is rendered as if it were already a percentage.
The same movement is stated in points in one place and in percent in another, so one of the two is the wrong unit.
A figure's scale came from its magnitude rather than from a declaration.
The rendered digits multiplied by the declared scale do not give the parsed value.
A claim's unit and its comparison form disagree: a percent unit carrying a point change, or a points unit carrying a percent change.
A figure's unit is unknown or absent, which puts it outside the unit checks.

the change is rendered as an unsigned magnitude, so the direction word is the only statement of direction and there is nothing to contradict
the two levels behind this change are not both resolvable, so the point change and the percent change cannot be told apart
